title: Turn five messy commits into a reviewable branch
summary: Your branch has 'wip', 'fix', 'fix again' and a typo commit. Use interactive rebase to squash, reword and drop until the history says something honest.
mental_model: Interactive rebase hands you a todo list — one line per commit, oldest first — and then replays the commits according to whatever you wrote. You are not editing history in place; you are creating brand-new commits and moving the branch to them.
danger: Every rebased commit gets a new sha. If anyone else has pulled this branch, rewriting it forces them into a painful reconciliation. Rebase your own unpushed work freely; think hard before rewriting shared branches.

steps.title: Look at what you would be asking someone to review
steps.why: Five commits, three of which say nothing, one that commits a debug log by accident, and a typo in the last message. Nobody can review this, and `git bisect` cannot use it either.

steps.title: Read the todo list rebase would give you
steps.why: This is exactly what `git rebase -i main` opens in your editor: one line per commit, oldest at the top, each starting with a command word. `pick` means keep it as is.
steps.expect: Five pick lines — the raw material of the rebase.

steps.title: Drop the accidental debug log commit first
steps.why: Deleting a line from the todo list drops that commit entirely, as if it was never written — its changes go with it. Do this before squashing: order matters, because `fixup` folds a commit into whatever line sits above it, and you do not want good code folded into a commit you are about to delete.
steps.expect: Four commits become three, and debug.log is gone from the tree.

verify.label: debug.log is no longer in the tree

steps.title: Squash the fix commits into the real one
steps.why: `squash` folds a commit into the one above it and opens an editor for a combined message; `fixup` does the same but throws the folded message away — which is right for a commit called 'fix'. The dashboard scripts the todo editor here; `-i` on your own machine just opens it in your editor instead.
steps.expect: Both 'fix' commits are gone; their code lives inside the first commit.

verify.label: the branch is down to two commits
the folded-in code survived the squash

steps.title: Reword the two remaining messages
steps.why: A commit message is the only documentation that travels with the change forever. `reword` replays the commit untouched and reopens just its message. Here we set both messages non-interactively.

env.GIT_EDITOR: sh -c 'if grep -q wip "$1" 2>/dev/null || grep -q Documnet "$1" 2>/dev/null; then if grep -q wip "$1"; then echo "Add dosing with input validation" > "$1"; else echo "Document the dosing feature" > "$1"; fi; fi' --

verify.label: no wip or typo messages remain

steps.title: Confirm the code survived the rewrite
steps.why: Rebase changed every sha on this branch, but the final tree should be identical apart from the dropped debug log. Diffing the branch against main is how you prove a rewrite was honest.

steps.title: The everyday shortcut: --autosquash
steps.why: In real work you rarely hand-edit the todo. Commit a follow-up with `git commit --fixup=<sha>` and later `git rebase -i --autosquash main` pre-arranges the list for you. This is the habit worth stealing.

verify.label: the branch is down to two clean commits
verify.hint: fold the fix commits in, drop the debug log commit

verify.label: no throwaway or misspelled commit messages remain
the accidental debug log never made it into the branch
the validation code from the squashed commits survived
verify.hint: squashing must keep the code and lose only the noise

pitfalls: Rebasing a branch that others have pulled forces everyone else to recover manually. Rewrite only what is still yours.
If a rebase hits a conflict it pauses mid-flight: resolve, `git add`, then `git rebase --continue` — never `git commit`.
`git rebase --abort` returns you to exactly where you started, at any point before the rebase finishes.
The reflog records the pre-rebase position, so even a rebase you regret is recoverable with `git reset --hard HEAD@{n}`.
cheatsheet: open the todo list for every commit since base
keep / change message / stop and amend
fold into the commit above, with / without its message
mark a commit as a fix for an earlier one
resume after a conflict / give up safely
